reason: Registered because the epistolary frame is genuinely Pauline and this is the phrase a reader will reach for. 'Dearly beloved' occurs in nine KJV verses — Jeremiah 12:7 and eight in the epistles, of which Philippians 4:1 ('my brethren dearly beloved and longed for … my dearly beloved') and 2 Timothy 1:2 ('my dearly beloved son') are the closest in form to Helaman's 'my dearly beloved brother, Moroni'. No one of the eight can be the source, and the vocative is the standing form of address in this correspondence (compare Alma 54 and 58). The chapter's Pauline link is filed at 56:2 on 'our warfare', which is a singleton; this is the same observation without a verse attached to it.

sharedText: did march at the head of these two thousand young men
reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection. 'I Helaman, did march at the head of these two thousand young men' repeats Alma 53:22's 'Helaman did march at the head of his two thousand stripling soldiers' almost word for word, and 53:22 is where the borrowing is adjudicated — on 'stripling', a KJV singleton at 1 Samuel 17:56 and the David typology the whole Ammonite sequence is built on. Helaman's letter is retelling the same march from the inside, so the repetition is the writer quoting his own narrative rather than the King James Bible a second time. Sent to 53:22, and see 56:57, where the word itself returns.

The second of 2 Corinthians 10:4's two distinctive nouns, and it will not carry a row of its own: 'strong holds' occurs in nineteen KJV verses, most of them David's wilderness refuges or the fortresses of Moab, and the Book of Mormon war narrative uses the term throughout for a fortified city. What makes it worth registering is its company — Alma 56 has both 'our warfare' (a KJV singleton) and 'strong holds' from the one Pauline verse that joins them, nineteen verses apart. Filed as a cross-reference to the link at 56:2, where the argument is made.

'They might catch us in their snare' is the chapter's one hunting metaphor and the KJV has several that would fit — Jeremiah 5:26's 'they lay wait, as he that setteth snares; they set a trap, they catch men', Psalm 35:8's net that catches the man who hid it, Psalm 10:9's lion that catches the poor in his net. None of them is verbally closer than the single word 'snare', and 'in their snare' occurs in no KJV verse at all. The same judgement was made at Alma 55:31 against Psalm 141:9. Registered so that the two snare verses of this pair of chapters are both accounted for.

'Took courage' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:8 (Asa, on hearing a prophecy) and Acts 28:15 (Paul, on meeting the brethren at Appii forum), and a two-verse count would ordinarily be enough to look at. It is not enough here for two reasons. The Book of Mormon has made the phrase its own — it occurs a dozen times from 1 Nephi 4:35 onward, usually as 'his heart did take courage' — and Alma 56:52's clause is a near-verbatim repetition of Alma 52:24, 'when the Lamanites saw that he began to flee, they took courage and pursued them with vigor', which is the same feigned retreat four chapters earlier. Both KJV instances are moreover of a godly man heartened by God's word or God's people, and both Book of Mormon instances are of the Lamanite army heartened by a retreat that is a trap.

'The remainder I took and joined them to my stripling Ammonites.' The word is a KJV singleton and it is the strongest single-word borrowing in this part of the book, but it is adjudicated at Alma 53:22, where it first enters and where the David typology that licenses it is argued. This is the same narrator using his own established name for the same two thousand men, four verses after calling them 'those young men'. Sent to 53:22.
